rv.q: Luckily, it offers great pleasure along with its factoids.
Others, too, might welcome that sense of comfort in a production of grandeur and heart.

Nevertheless, many might prefer a visit to one of the country’s natural history museums that offer similarly spectacular and immersive video experiences—minus the clanking dialogue and creaking mechanics of “Redwood.”
But that earnestness is tough to sustain.

It makes for an intimate and vulnerable performance, even as an expensive curtain of LED screens (video design by Hana S. Kim, scenic design by Jason Ardizzone-West) bathes the stage action, transforming the Nederlander Theatre into starscapes and forests like a theatricalized Artechouse.
But, wow, is this clunky show on the nose with all that stuff.
Even as Menzel's Jesse climbs to new physical heights, the lumbering Redwood brings her down.
There’s still a sentimental solipsism in Redwood, an uneasy aspect of emotional tourism smothered in a broadside of throw-pillow truisms on connection, growth, and healing.
As always, Menzel is pure magic.
If that sounds a bit … shallow for a concept, well, yes.
Too bad the Broadway show named after the wooden giant is a toothpick.
By then, whatever initial misgivings it may have produced, “Redwood” is likely to have wormed its way into your heart.
The stagecraft, performances, and the visuals will last and no doubt offer a roadmap for future projection-heavy productions.
But the show itself hangs from a story that’s as thin as a reed, making for a sometimes-lumbering musical that tends to sag under the weight of its nearly two-hour runtime.
That awesome and fascinating tree turns “Redwood” into a kind of poetry, albeit a lyrical poem rather than a narrative one.
Despite any sympathy we might have for Jesse, she is not all that interesting a character.

Unfortunately, it’s too often in the service of a generic pop-sounding, lyrically banal score by musical theatre newcomer Kate Diaz, with too many songs that simply reinforce emotions that have already been expressed and do little to advance the barely-there plot.
Too bad the monumental wilderness conjured by the designers overwhelms the twig of a story about an unhappy woman fleeing her demons.
But the show never reaches the heights to which it aspires, except of the vertical kind.
That same could be said for the show itself.
But for a musical that should soar, it most often feels dreadfully earthbound.
Redwood has the seeds of a moving story about finding healing and community among the most unexpected people (and trees), but it still has room to grow.
Redwood, in the end, can’t find the forest for the trees.
But none of its ideas or characters are given space to coalesce into anything meaningful, with blandly inspirational songs crowding out an ecosystem that would better thrive on more organic soil.

Getting Jesse up that tree, on the other hand, involves such contortions of character and logic that the whole endeavor is less a flight of fancy, or even derangement, than it is hopelessly contrived.
With so much talent and effort put into a production, it is startling to see how far off the mark this production landed.
Well, it’s a lovely thought to end with if by now you are not lying, whimpering and exhausted, on Redwood’s forest floor of confected conflict and overstated metaphors.
But all the vocal pyrotechnics on Broadway can’t help this Redwood grow.
But agony and art don’t necessarily always combine to soothe our pangs, especially when the former doesn’t endow the latter with enough truth.
To say that Guingona is brilliant in the role of Rothko is an understatement, and that is really a failure at finding the right words for this portrayal.

Redwood is a show with a lot of heart, unique in its desire to show a story of calmness and healing, for the most part, pretty far away from deadlines, time crunches, and the typical story telling structure of a person who knows where they’re going and is prepared to risk everything to get there.

And while I have liked Menzel in many of her roles, her performance here feels like her most complete as Jesse bares her soul, exuding pain and joy with powerful vocals and impressive athletics (I guess the height never bothered her anyway).
Themes of love, loss, grief and acceptance are present but not explored in enough depth
Strong performances led by Idina Menzel give this musical its beating heart.

The trunk of the titular redwood is a wide semi-circle that extends from the floor all the way up to the stage-lights above. Meanwhile, immersive projections on the back walls create the lush backdrop of a Northern California forest.
Redwood is worth seeing simply for the strength of Menzel’s vision—though the ensemble definitely each get their time to shine, they never feel fully fulfilled.

cn.t: Critics find *Redwood* a well-intentioned but dramatically shallow vehicle for Idina Menzel's powerhouse vocals. The stunning tree set and projections impress, but the grief-centered story lacks emotional depth and memorable songs.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.

vr.q: I was actually a bit bored during the show because the problem is our main character... she didn't have a clear want... I just had a hard time rooting for her
I'm willing to get behind the show being primarily a vehicle for Idina and the rest of the stellar cast, but I found the material kind of hard to invest in.
A musical needs two things to be successful. It needs a good story and good songs. And I would contend disappointingly that this doesn't really have either.
